cards.title: Counting to three in Russian
cards.body: In Russian, the numbers one through three are один (odin, pronounced "ah-DEEN"), два (dva, pronounced "dvah"), and три (tri, pronounced "tree"). Because Russian is an Indo-European language, these numbers share an ancient ancestry with English "two" and "three", Spanish "dos" and "tres", and Sanskrit "dva" and "tri". Counting basic objects in Russian offers an immediate window into the shared roots of languages spanning Europe and South Asia.

cards.title: How a small red fruit gave us the word "tawny"
cards.body: The word "tawny", describing an orange-brown or brownish-yellow hue, traces back to the Old French word "tané", meaning tanned or tawny. This derives from the Medieval Latin "tannare" (to tan hides using crushed tree bark). Ultimately, the root connects to the Celtic term for oak bark. Relatedly, "tangerine" comes from the port of Tangier in Morocco, but "tawny" has entirely separate woodland roots tied to the medieval leather trade.

cards.title: How to say "excuse me" in Japanese
cards.body: To get someone's attention, squeeze through a crowd, or offer a light apology in Japanese, use すみません (sumimasen, pronounced "soo-mee-mah-sen"). Derived from the verb 済む (sumu, meaning to end or be settled), it literally means "it does not end"—acknowledging that an obligation or inconvenience cannot easily be repaid. It is one of Japan's most versatile everyday phrases, functioning as "sorry", "excuse me", and even a polite "thank you".

cards.title: How counting steps gave us the "mile"
cards.body: The English word "mile" traces directly to ancient Rome. Roman legions measured long distances by counting pairs of marching steps. The Latin term "mille passus" literally translates to "a thousand paces", where one pace (passus) equaled two full strides (left foot to left foot again), measuring roughly five Roman feet. The ancient Roman mile spanned about 1,480 meters (4,856 feet), slightly shorter than today's standard statute mile of 5,280 feet.

cards.title: Greeting someone with peace in Hindi
cards.body: The standard greeting across the Hindi-speaking world is नमस्ते (namaste, pronounced "nuh-muh-stay") or the more formal नमस्कार (namaskar, pronounced "nuh-muhs-kar"). Rooted in ancient Sanskrit, the term joins "namas" (meaning bow or obeisance) and "te" (meaning to you). Uttered with palms pressed together at chest height and a slight bow, the phrase literally translates to "I bow to you", symbolizing mutual respect and honoring the presence of the other person.

guesses.prompt: How many double-stride paces made up one ancient Roman mile ("mille passus")?
guesses.explanation: A Roman mile was defined as exactly 1,000 double-stride paces (mille passus), measuring around 4,856 modern feet.

misconceptions.claim: The English word 'mile' was originally defined as 5,280 paces.
misconceptions.explanation: The word 'mile' comes from the Latin 'mille passus', meaning exactly 1,000 paces. The 5,280-foot definition was codified much later by English statute.
